description: Prepared evergreen educational queue; factual claims require periodic rechecking; no claims of hands-on testing

articles.title: Where should you put a Wi-Fi router?
articles.dek: A room-by-room guide to improving wireless coverage before spending money on new hardware.
sections: Start with the actual problem

A router's position can make a noticeable difference to coverage, but it cannot fix every slow connection. Before moving equipment, check whether the problem affects every device or only a particular room. Test the same device near the router and again where performance is poor. If the speed and reliability improve nearby, wireless coverage is worth investigating.

Also check whether the internet provider has reported an outage. A device can be connected to Wi-Fi while its internet connection is unavailable. Fixing Wi-Fi placement will not repair a provider outage.
Choose a central, open location

For many homes, a reasonably central, elevated position gives the router more opportunity to reach rooms in different directions. Placing it behind a metal cabinet, inside a closet or close to large obstructions can interfere with the path between the router and devices.

You do not have to put the router in the geometric center of the house at any cost. Consider where people actually need connectivity, where the incoming connection is located, electrical safety and whether its antennas can be positioned according to the manufacturer's instructions.
Know what walls and floors change

Walls, floors and other building materials can attenuate wireless signals. The impact depends on the material, thickness, frequency band and layout. A signal that crosses multiple dense barriers may be less reliable than one with a clearer path. If you use equipment with multiple bands, experiment with the manufacturer-recommended settings before making broad changes.

A simple way to compare locations is to use the same device, stand in the same test spots and repeat comparable tasks after each change. Keep notes on room, position and whether the problem improved. That is more informative than relying on a single test result.
Compare three low-cost improvements

First, move the router out of an enclosure and away from large metal objects if practical. Second, position it where it is less obstructed by furniture and high-traffic household equipment. Third, if your home is larger or has difficult construction, consider wired access points or a properly configured mesh system only after confirming a coverage gap.
Avoid buying a new router simply because a speed-test score is disappointing. The limiting factor might be your internet plan, local device, an overcrowded channel or the destination service.
When placement is not enough

If the device is still slow near the router, investigate internet service, hardware condition and network configuration. If the router is far from a room and moving it is impractical, a wired Ethernet connection may be the most predictable option for fixed devices.

Never factory reset network equipment as a first troubleshooting step. Resetting can erase passwords, network settings and provider-specific configuration. Follow official instructions, and keep a record of symptoms before contacting support.
Quick decision checklist

Test two devices and two locations. Check for a provider outage. Move the router out of enclosed or obstructed locations. Repeat comparable tests. Only consider buying additional networking hardware if you have evidence of a coverage problem.

articles.title: kW vs. kWh: what your electricity bill actually measures
articles.dek: Understand power and energy, see the math, and estimate costs with a realistic example.
sources: U.S. Department of Energy — Estimating appliance energy use
sections: The short answer

A kilowatt (kW) describes a rate of power use. A kilowatt-hour (kWh) measures how much energy is used over time. Utility bills commonly include charges based on kilowatt-hours consumed. The distinction matters because two appliances with the same power rating can use very different amounts of energy depending on how long they run.
Convert watts into kilowatts

Power is often stated in watts. Divide a watt value by 1,000 to express the same power in kilowatts. A 100-watt load is 0.1 kW. A 1,500-watt load is 1.5 kW. The rating on an appliance may describe a maximum or nominal draw, not its continuous measured average.

If a device cycles on and off, such as a refrigerator or heater, simple nameplate estimates may overstate or understate actual consumption. A compatible energy meter or manufacturer-provided consumption data can make the estimate more useful.
Convert power and time into energy

Energy in kilowatt-hours is power in kilowatts multiplied by running time in hours. A hypothetical steady 100-watt device run for eight hours would use 0.8 kWh. Over 30 identical days, that would total 24 kWh.
A device run at twice the power for half the time can consume the same energy if all other factors are equal. That is why wattage alone cannot tell you what a device will cost over a month.
Estimate the part of the bill related to energy

Multiply estimated kWh by the relevant electricity rate in dollars per kWh. At an example rate of $0.15/kWh, 24 kWh would represent $3.60 in energy charges. Actual bills can also include fixed charges, seasonal rates, taxes, time-of-use pricing, demand charges or other utility-specific adjustments.

The site's calculator estimates energy cost, not your full utility bill. Use the exact rate and billing period from your utility when possible; avoid treating an arbitrary national average as your household price.
Why actual use can differ

Heating elements, compressors, electronic power supplies and other systems may change their electricity draw during operation. Standby modes can consume energy, and operating conditions matter. For a more accurate estimate, measure average consumption over a representative period instead of assuming the device draws its maximum wattage constantly.
Use the free tool

Open the electricity cost calculator on this site and try multiple wattage, hour and rate assumptions. Compare estimates before deciding whether a new device or a change in habits is financially worthwhile.

articles.title: Why is my phone charging slowly?
articles.dek: A practical checklist for checking cables, adapters, heat and charging settings safely.
sources: USB Implementers Forum — USB Power Delivery
sections: Separate normal slowdowns from faults

Many devices vary their charging speed throughout a charging session. Charging may slow as the battery approaches full, or when the device is warm. One measurement at an arbitrary battery percentage does not prove that a cable or adapter is defective.

If a device reports a charging or temperature warning, follow the device manufacturer's instructions before testing anything else. Stop using damaged, swollen, wet or unusually hot charging equipment.
Start with the power source

A computer USB port, a low-power adapter and a capable USB Power Delivery charger can offer very different charging capability. Check your phone's documented supported charging methods and compare them to the adapter specifications.
A higher number printed on a charger does not mean the phone will continuously draw that power. The phone, charger, cable and charging conditions all play a role.
Check the cable without guessing

USB-C describes connector shape, not a guarantee of particular current, transfer speed or charging protocol. Some cables are unsuitable for high-power or specialized uses. Read the printed rating or manufacturer specification rather than assuming all USB-C cables are identical.
Try a known-good manufacturer-compatible cable if one is available. Do not repair or continue using a cable with exposed conductors, melted insulation or damaged connectors.
Consider temperature, apps and settings

Charging can be affected by thermal management, wireless charging alignment and device settings. Heavy activities such as gaming or video recording may consume power while the device is charging and make the percentage rise more slowly.

If supported, check the device's battery health and optimized charging information. Device menus vary, so rely on the manufacturer manual for the exact setting names rather than following a generic sequence of taps.
When to seek service

Repeated unexpected shutdowns, excessive heat, physical battery damage or persistent charging errors warrant support from the device maker or an authorized service provider. Do not attempt to puncture or dismantle lithium-ion batteries.

For an ordinary slow-charge complaint, document the adapter, cable, battery level, temperature and approximate charge time before contacting support. Those details help avoid replacing perfectly good accessories.
Buying checklist

Before buying a new accessory, confirm the phone's supported input, charger output and the cable's verified rating. Compare a known-good setup first. Favor clear technical specifications and reliable return policies over unsupported speed claims.

articles.title: How large a power bank do you really need?
articles.dek: Understand watt-hours, capacity claims, losses and travel considerations before choosing portable charging.
sections: Start with your actual use case

A small battery pack that tops up a phone during commuting serves a different purpose from a large pack intended to keep multiple devices operating through a trip. Consider which devices you will charge, whether they need USB-C Power Delivery and how often you will have access to an outlet.
Do not choose solely by the biggest milliamp-hour number on the package. That single number does not describe output voltage, conversion losses or whether a device can negotiate the power it needs.
Understand mAh and Wh

Milliamp-hours (mAh) describe electric charge capacity at a stated voltage. Watt-hours (Wh) represent stored energy. To estimate watt-hours from a specified nominal voltage, multiply amp-hours by volts. Because devices use different nominal voltages, two mAh figures cannot always be compared directly.
For illustration, a 10,000 mAh pack rated at a nominal 3.7 volts corresponds to about 37 Wh of nominal stored energy (10 Ah × 3.7 V). This is not a claim about usable USB output energy.
Why you will not receive all the stated energy

Voltage conversion, heat, cable and connector losses, internal reserve, device charging circuitry and environmental conditions affect what reaches the connected device. For that reason, advertised capacity is not equivalent to the exact amount that can be delivered to your phone.

A useful comparison is the manufacturer's declared Wh rating alongside supported USB output ratings, physical size, quality and warranty. Real delivered capacity must be measured under specified conditions.
Check output capability separately

A battery pack's total capacity and maximum output power answer different questions. Capacity relates to how long it may supply energy; output rating relates to whether it can power or charge a particular device at the desired rate. Check the laptop or phone's requirements, the pack's port ratings and the cable's capability together.

Multiple devices plugged into one pack may share a total output budget. Look for manufacturer documentation that explains simultaneous charging limits rather than assuming every port reaches its advertised individual maximum.
Air travel and safety

Airline and aviation rules apply to lithium batteries and power banks, and restrictions depend on their watt-hour ratings and other conditions. Consult the FAA PackSafe rules and your airline before traveling. Do not rely on a generic social-media chart as your sole source.
Stop using a battery pack that is visibly swollen, leaking, damaged or abnormally hot. Keep it away from excessive heat and follow the manufacturer's handling instructions.
An efficient purchase decision

Write down device power needs, desired number of recharges, size/weight preference and travel restrictions. Compare verified Wh and output specs, then decide whether the extra capacity is worth carrying. More capacity is not always a better fit.

articles.title: 2.4 GHz vs. 5 GHz Wi-Fi: which should you use?
articles.dek: A practical guide to coverage, congestion, compatibility and choosing a Wi-Fi band.
sections: Different bands solve different needs

Many home networks support both 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz wireless bands. Broadly, 2.4 GHz often offers better range through obstacles in typical conditions, while 5 GHz can offer more channel capacity and higher throughput under suitable conditions. Actual results depend on the router, client, congestion, walls and local regulations.
A band name does not guarantee a speed. A poorly placed router on an uncongested band may outperform a newer one operating under heavy interference. Test your real devices where you use them.
When 2.4 GHz can be helpful

Some older or simpler connected devices support only 2.4 GHz. That band can also be practical where coverage matters more than peak data transfer. However, it is widely shared with other equipment and nearby wireless networks, so interference can still make performance poor.
If a smart-home accessory refuses to join the network, consult its manufacturer's setup instructions. Avoid disabling important security settings as a workaround.
When 5 GHz can be helpful

For devices relatively close to an access point and able to support it, 5 GHz often works well for high-throughput activities. The higher-frequency signal can weaken more over some walls and obstacles than a lower-frequency alternative.

It is not necessary to manually manage every device. Many routers use automatic band steering; manufacturer defaults may work well. Use simple comparisons rather than assuming the higher-numbered band always wins.
A fair comparison method

Use the same client and destination, test in the same room at roughly the same time, and repeat tests more than once. Look for repeatable differences in responsiveness and reliability, not just one peak result.
If problems occur only in a far room, think about router position or network coverage before assuming the band is incorrectly configured.
About Wi-Fi 6 and other names

Wi-Fi generation names describe sets of capabilities and are not interchangeable with frequency bands. Some newer equipment supports additional bands, but both the router and client must support the relevant features to benefit. Consult official manufacturer specifications for compatibility.
The practical answer

Leave band selection automatic when it works. If a specific device has a repeated problem, test the supported alternatives, verify security settings and document the outcome. Change one setting at a time so you can tell what made a difference.

articles.title: How much does an LED light bulb cost to run?
articles.dek: Use wattage and hours to compare lighting energy costs without confusing brightness and power.
sources: U.S. Department of Energy — Lighting choices to save money
U.S. Department of Energy — Estimating energy use
sections: Start with the actual wattage

Brightness and electricity use are not the same measure. The watt number describes the bulb's power use under specified conditions, while lumens describe the amount of visible light emitted. For comparing how much lighting costs to operate, the watt rating and hours of use matter most.
Read the specific lamp packaging or documentation instead of assuming all bulbs marketed as the same brightness consume the same number of watts.
A useful calculation

A hypothetical 9-watt lamp running five hours a day for 30 days consumes 1.35 kWh: 9 ÷ 1,000 × 5 × 30. At an example price of $0.15 per kWh, the energy portion of the monthly cost is about $0.20. Actual rates, run times and power use will differ.
A full household electricity bill often includes fixed fees and other charges; this example covers the bulb's estimated energy consumption alone.
Comparing two options fairly

If two light sources provide comparable useful illumination, comparing their electrical wattages is a reasonable starting point for energy costs. But wattage is not the only purchase consideration: brightness, beam direction, fit, color appearance, dimmer compatibility and expected lifespan matter too.
An inexpensive bulb that flickers with a particular dimmer or creates uncomfortable glare may be a poor purchase even if its running cost is low. Check compatibility and manufacturer recommendations.
How long the light is on matters

A light that runs for ten minutes a day has much less opportunity to affect energy costs than a light used for long evening hours. Estimate typical hours rather than multiplying every lamp by 24 hours.
For shared spaces or irregular schedules, take a representative week and note how often each light is used. That can make your assumptions more realistic.
Safety and compatibility

Use bulbs suited to the fixture's electrical and thermal ratings. Enclosed fixtures, outdoor locations and dimmers may have specific lamp requirements. Do not exceed the fixture's rated limits or modify electrical wiring without appropriate expertise.
Try the calculation yourself

Use the site's electricity cost calculator with your bulb's watts and your bill's rate. Then compare the estimated energy savings with the price of replacing a working bulb. This lets you decide based on your situation rather than an exaggerated savings claim.

articles.title: Wi-Fi connected but no internet? A practical troubleshooting guide
articles.dek: Find out whether the problem is your device, router, provider or public Wi-Fi sign-in before resetting settings.
sources: Microsoft Support — Fix Wi-Fi connection issues in Windows
Apple Support — If you can't connect to Wi-Fi on iPhone or iPad
Apple Support — Use captive Wi-Fi networks
sections: Why Wi-Fi can be connected while the internet is down

A Wi-Fi connection links your device to a nearby access point; it does not guarantee that the router or internet provider can reach websites. A device can therefore show strong signal bars while apps cannot load. First distinguish a complete outage from a single failed website or app. Try two unrelated sites and note the exact warning. If only one service fails while others work, investigate that service rather than immediately replacing equipment. A connection-status icon is useful evidence, but it is not a complete diagnosis.
Use two devices to locate the fault

Test a second phone or computer on the same Wi-Fi network. If both fail, investigate the router, modem and provider before changing either device. If only one fails, concentrate on that device. When possible, temporarily turn off Wi-Fi on a phone and test over cellular data, taking care not to use unexpected mobile data. If cellular works while every home Wi-Fi device fails, the websites are unlikely to be the shared cause. Record which devices and connections worked; this simple comparison often saves time and unnecessary purchases.
Check the provider and physical connection

Using cellular service if available, check your provider's official outage page or support channel. Look at the router and modem or fiber terminal for clearly labeled connection and alarm lights, interpreting them with the equipment manual. A working Wi-Fi light does not prove that the provider connection is healthy. Check accessible cables and power connections without opening equipment. Stop using damaged or unusually hot electrical accessories. If the provider reports an outage, wait for restoration rather than changing settings. Otherwise, follow the equipment maker's normal restart procedure and allow time to reconnect.
Restart safely; do not factory reset

A restart means switching equipment off and on as its manufacturer recommends. A factory reset is different: it can erase network names, passwords and customized provider settings. Do not press a recessed Reset button as a first troubleshooting step. If you have separate modem and router units, follow the provider's recommended restart order. Test the connection again before doing anything more complicated. If it returns, note what helped and stop changing settings. If it does not, keep the observations for a support call rather than repeating restarts indefinitely.
When only one device has the problem

Turn Wi-Fi off and on, reconnect to the correct network and restart the affected device. Check whether it works on another trusted Wi-Fi network. Windows users can run Microsoft's Network and Internet troubleshooter; iPhone and iPad users can inspect the Wi-Fi settings and any No Internet Connection message. Follow the linked official instructions because menus vary by operating-system version. Consider whether a recently enabled VPN, proxy, filtering app or security tool coincided with the problem. On managed work or school devices, ask the administrator before altering such settings or weakening protection.
Recognize DNS and IP-address clues

A device may reach its router but fail to translate website names into addresses, which can suggest a DNS problem. Microsoft documents checking network configuration, renewing an address and clearing the DNS resolver cache in Windows. An automatically assigned address beginning with 169.254 can indicate that the computer did not obtain the expected address through DHCP. Neither clue alone proves that the router is defective. Record existing settings before changing DNS or IP configuration. If your network uses fixed addresses, parental controls or business management, seek appropriate guidance rather than switching to arbitrary public DNS servers.
Public Wi-Fi may require a sign-in page

Hotels, airports and other public networks may let you join Wi-Fi but require a login or acceptance of terms before granting internet access. This is called a captive portal. Apple's guidance for iPhone and iPad is to select the network in Wi-Fi settings and wait for the login screen, or use Join Network when available. Use only the venue's legitimate portal; do not install unfamiliar certificates or profiles to make a hotspot work. Ask the venue for official instructions if the sign-in page never appears. This situation differs from a home broadband outage.
Escalate based on what the tests reveal

If several devices fail and the provider equipment shows an upstream problem, contact the provider with the outage time, indicator status and restart results. If one device fails on multiple otherwise-working networks, contact its manufacturer or IT support. Resetting network settings on an iPhone or iPad can remove saved Wi-Fi passwords and related cellular or VPN settings, so reserve it for later troubleshooting under Apple's instructions. If devices work near the router but not in a distant room, investigate wireless coverage instead. The goal is to isolate the failure before spending money, erasing settings or making disruptive changes.

articles.title: How much does a space heater cost to run? Calculate it before you plug in
articles.dek: Use your heater's wattage, actual running time and electricity rate to estimate daily and monthly costs, then check the safety rules that matter.
sources: U.S. Energy Information Administration — Measuring electricity
U.S. Energy Information Administration — Factors affecting electricity prices
U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission — Portable electric heater safety habits
U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission — Winter weather and portable heater safety
ENERGY STAR — Ductless heating and cooling
sections: The quick answer: watts, hours and your rate

A portable electric heater's running cost depends primarily on how much electrical power it draws, how long its heating element actually operates, and the price you pay per kilowatt-hour (kWh). A heater marked 1,500 watts draws about 1.5 kilowatts while operating at that rated input. At a purely illustrative electricity rate of $0.20 per kWh, one full-power hour costs about $0.30 in energy charges. Four full-power hours cost about $1.20. These are calculations, not measured results or a prediction of anyone's utility bill.

An adjustable thermostat complicates the estimate in a useful way: the heater may switch its heating element off after reaching the selected temperature. Four hours plugged in does not always mean four hours at full power. Start with the full-power estimate as a planning scenario, then refine it if you know the actual operating time.
Find the wattage before doing any math

Check the heater's rating label, manual or manufacturer specification for input power in watts (W). A unit may list different wattages for low and high settings; use the one you actually select. If the label lists electrical current and voltage instead, do not assume that multiplying those numbers gives an exact measured average power draw. The manufacturer's stated wattage is the safer starting point for a simple consumer estimate.

Do not confuse a heater's physical size, marketing name or advertised room coverage with electricity use. Two differently styled heaters can have the same rated wattage. Likewise, a timer setting tells you how long a unit is permitted to operate, not necessarily how long its heating element is energized.
Calculate cost with a three-step formula

First, divide watts by 1,000 to convert power to kilowatts. Second, multiply kilowatts by the hours the heater is drawing that power to obtain kilowatt-hours. Third, multiply kilowatt-hours by your electricity price in dollars per kWh. In one line: estimated energy cost = (watts ÷ 1,000) × full-power hours × electricity rate. The U.S. Energy Information Administration explains that watts measure power while kilowatt-hours measure electricity used over time.

For a monthly estimate, multiply the daily energy cost by the number of days used. Keep units visible as you calculate: 1,500 W ÷ 1,000 = 1.5 kW; 1.5 kW × 4 hours = 6 kWh; 6 kWh × $0.20/kWh = $1.20. Multiply $1.20 by 30 days to get $36 in hypothetical energy charges. The math assumes identical use every day, which rarely happens exactly.
Compare common settings without confusing them with measured use

At the same illustrative $0.20/kWh rate, a 750-watt setting running continuously for four hours uses 3 kWh and costs $0.60. A 1,000-watt setting over four full-power hours uses 4 kWh and costs $0.80. A 1,500-watt setting for four full-power hours uses 6 kWh and costs $1.20. Over 30 days of identical use, those scenarios correspond to $18, $24 and $36 in energy charges, respectively.

These examples do not mean the lower setting always costs less to maintain the same room temperature. A lower setting might run longer, while a higher setting might cycle off sooner. Room size, insulation, drafts, outdoor temperature, thermostat placement and the amount of heat already supplied by the home's heating system all influence the result.
What a thermostat changes—and what it does not

Suppose a 1,500-watt heater is switched on for four hours, but its heating element runs for only two of those hours because the thermostat cycles it on and off. Ignoring small additional consumption from controls or a fan, the heating element uses approximately 1.5 kW × 2 hours = 3 kWh, or $0.60 at the example rate. That is half the four-hour continuous-heating scenario.

Do not assume a 50 percent duty cycle just because a heater has a thermostat. During a cold spell, a heater in a drafty room may run almost continuously; in a well-insulated room it may cycle much less. If you cannot establish actual energized time, show a range of scenarios instead of presenting one precise monthly cost as fact. Never defeat safety controls to obtain a measurement.
Use the right electricity price from your bill

Look for your utility's price per kWh, then determine whether that number represents only an energy-supply charge or includes additional variable delivery charges. Some customers face time-of-use prices, seasonal rates, tiered usage charges or separate fixed fees. A fixed monthly customer charge usually will not change because you run one more appliance, but variable charges can. The EIA documents that electricity prices vary by location and customer type.

If your bill includes several variable per-kWh components, adding the applicable components may provide a better estimate of the extra cost than using only the advertised supply rate. If you have time-of-use pricing, estimate hours in each rate period separately and add them. Do not treat the example $0.20/kWh as a current national average or a price guaranteed for your home.
Ceramic, oil-filled and infrared: does the style change the bill?

Portable ceramic fan heaters, oil-filled radiators and many infrared room heaters commonly rely on electric resistance to create heat. At the same actual electrical energy use, there is no magic efficiency bonus that makes one resistance heater deliver dramatically more total heat into the room. Their differences often concern how quickly and where warmth is felt, whether a fan moves air, and how a thermostat manages operation.

An oil-filled heater does not burn its internal oil as fuel; the oil stores and distributes heat. An infrared heater can make a person or nearby surface feel warm without warming all the room air equally. Either may be more comfortable for a particular situation, but comfort is not a substitute for measured energy consumption. Compare wattage, safety features and appropriate use rather than relying on unsupported 'pennies a day' advertising.
Will a space heater save money compared with central heating?

Sometimes, but only under specific conditions. Heating one occupied room while safely reducing the heat delivered elsewhere might lower overall heating demand. Running a portable heater on top of an unchanged central heating schedule usually adds electricity consumption rather than replacing it. The outcome depends on your main heating fuel, equipment efficiency, home layout, heat loss, electricity tariff and whether other rooms can actually be kept cooler without causing problems.

Electric resistance heaters and heat pumps should not be treated as interchangeable. A heat pump moves heat instead of generating it solely through resistance, which can reduce electricity use for comparable heating needs under appropriate conditions. ENERGY STAR describes ductless heat pumps as an efficient option for suitable homes. For a single cold room, first check drafts, blocked vents and thermostat settings before assuming a second heater is the least expensive fix.
Safety is not optional when choosing a location or outlet

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission advises keeping all sides of a portable heater at least three feet from bedding, curtains, furniture, papers and other combustible items. Put it on a stable, level surface where children or pets will not knock it over. Keep it away from water. Plug an electric portable heater directly into a suitable wall outlet—not a power strip or extension cord—and do not route its cord beneath a rug or carpet.

Never leave a portable heater running while you sleep or when it is unattended. If its plug or cord becomes hot, disconnect it and seek qualified service; if the wall outlet itself is hot, contact a qualified electrician. Do not use a heater with a damaged cord, plug or housing. Before using an older or secondhand model, check official recall information. A bargain electricity estimate is never a reason to ignore these precautions.
A five-minute decision checklist

Write down the heater's rated watts and the setting you plan to use. Choose a realistic number of full-power hours per day, not just the number of hours it is plugged in. Find the relevant variable price per kWh on your bill. Calculate daily and monthly energy cost for a high-use and a lower-use scenario. Finally, check whether the heater can be positioned and connected safely without extension cords, power strips or combustible materials nearby.

Use Practical Pick's free electricity cost calculator to compare wattage, hours and your own rate; the result is an energy-only estimate, not a forecast of your entire utility bill. If the predicted cost is too high, consider addressing drafts or evaluating your existing heating system rather than shopping for a supposedly miraculous resistance heater. The best decision combines realistic energy math, comfort and safe operation.
